extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century American literature; students and scholars of Whitman
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and reminiscences from Walt Whitman's Specimen Days — observational diary-essays on theater, nature, war, manufacture, and poetry. Not a how-to or guideline page but contains evaluative remarks about acting, manufacture, poetry, and soldiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great acting — concentration of passion and spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: "instant and tremendous concentration of passion in his delineations overwhelm'd his audience... He was singularly spontaneous and fluctuating; in the same part each rendering differ'd from any and all others. He had no stereotyped positions and made no arbitrary requirements on his fellow-performers. He knew all stage points thoroughly..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman's account treats the actor's power to concentrate passion and to vary each performance (spontaneity, fluctuation) as central marks of excellence; technical mastery of stage points combined with avoidance of fixed, stereotyped poses and generosity toward fellow actors are highlighted as practical indicators of superior acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reception — sustained attention and quick rapport
rubrics_metrics.description: "audiences that paid a good actor or an interesting play the compliment of more sustain'd attention or quicker rapport..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained attention and rapid, strong rapport from an audience (e.g., prolonged ovations, 'tempests' of hand-clapping) are presented as observable measures of a performance's success and an actor's impact on a public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plate glass quality — clarity, size, finish, luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman describes the works as producing plate glass "the clearest and largest, best, and the most finish'd and luxurious in the world" and goes on to detail the sand, melting, pot, rolling, annealing, and polishing processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for assessing plate glass in the account are optical clarity, large size, high finish, and luxurious appearance; Whitman also signals attention to manufacturing process (raw sand quality, pot shape/color, annealing, polishing) and the striking visual/aesthetic effects of molten material and final slabs as part of quality judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's value — universality and moral/aesthetic centrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whitman observes that all poets and poetic utterance are a dominant moral factor in humanity's progress and that "all poetry thus has ... more features of resemblance than difference," suggesting a shared center across ages and cultures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than enumerating technical metrics, Whitman advances a philosophical evaluative claim: the worth of poetry lies in its universal, unifying, religious/aesthetic power for humanity. This functions as a high-level criterion for valuing poetic work — its moral and aesthetic influence and its relation to a broader poetic tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier/regiment assessment — physical bearing and appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: On seeing the 195th Pennsylvania and other troops he notes "so hardy, candid, bright American looks, all weather-beaten, and with warm clothes" and calls out the "fine physical appearance of the whole body" as remarkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman uses observable physical traits (hardiness, weather-beaten looks, bearing, dress) and demeanor as informal indicators of a regiment's quality and 'practical' character; these visual impressions are treated as meaningful measures of soldierly fitness and civic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handwriting by wounded soldiers — aesthetic merit and characteristic slant
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding specimens of left-hand writing by soldiers: "A great many of the specimens are written in a beautiful manner. All are good. The writing in nearly all cases slants backward instead of forward. One piece...was made by holding the pen in his mouth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman records aesthetic judgment (beauty, overall quality) of adaptive handwriting by maimed soldiers and notes characteristic features (backward slant) and extraordinary methods (mouth-writing). These observations implicitly form criteria for valuing adaptive skill and effort in bodily-disabled writing.
